description: We are NeuraVesta, a multidisciplinary team of developers, AI enthusiasts, researchers, and product builders. We are building GRAVIFIRE to make NASA microgravity fire research easier to explore and understand. Our skills include full-stack development, AI, data analysis, QA, UI/UX, and 3D visualization. We welcome people skilled in space science, ML, WebGL, design, video editing, and scientific storytelling.
summary:
GRAVIFIRE is a super intelligence (SI) powered web dashboard and evidence engine that turns NASA’s scattered microgravity combustion experiments (BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-II) into clear fire safety answers. It is built for the fire safety engineer deciding what is safe to fly, and also helps researchers and students.

It answers the “Flame in Freefall” challenge with one question: can Earth fire tests be trusted in space? Users pick a material and mission condition, compare Earth and microgravity results side by side, and receive a verdict of Supported, Contradicted or Insufficient Evidence. Every number traces back to its source file and row. When evidence is missing, GRAVIFIRE refuses to guess, shows the gap, and names the next experiment to run. EMBER, our SI research assistant, explains any verdict by citing the original NASA data, and a game-like ISV Vesta spacecraft set in 2038 shows it all in use.

In a blind test with an entire NASA flight hidden, the engine made zero false confirmations. We also found that PDMS burns completely on Earth but ignites and then stalls in microgravity.

This matters because Moon and Mars habitats will use oxygen-enriched air where materials burn more easily. GRAVIFIRE shows what we know, what we do not, and what NASA should test next.
details:
GRAVIFIRE is an interactive research and learning platform that makes NASA combustion research easier to discover, understand and trace to its original sources. Built by Team NeuraVesta, it helps researchers, students and educators see what fire experiments reveal, and what they cannot establish, about combustion in different environments.

Users choose a mission context (spacecraft, lunar habitat or Mars habitat) and a fire-safety objective: prevention, detection or suppression. GRAVIFIRE ranks relevant NASA investigations with transparent, deterministic scoring. Users then inspect source records, compare experimental conditions with hypothetical mission settings, and follow citations and provenance. Every comparison marks conditions as matched, mismatched or unknown. EMBER, our evidence assistant, answers supported questions through deterministic retrieval and structured responses.

Mission Control is a fictional 2038 campaign aboard ISV Vesta. A Fire Safety Officer reviews the Aegis-1 mission manifest (for example, a Mars habitat at about 0.38 g), investigates materials, and confronts conditions the NASA archive cannot answer. A realistic mission, built for a future need: crews heading to the Moon and Mars will live in atmospheres and gravity levels where most flammability knowledge, gathered on Earth, may not transfer. It needs no custom hardware, runs in a browser, and keeps fictional scenarios clearly separate from NASA observations.

How it uses NASA data

GRAVIFIRE works directly with NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data from BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-II. Experimental tables, run records, imagery and raw video are normalized into one evidence store (BASS-II alone offers 129 searchable run records). Dashboards show conditions, raw NASA video and source records side by side. Every record carries its repository, investigation, source file, source row and SHA-256 hash, with a “Real NASA data” label. Missing measurements, such as airflow, pressure or outcome, are shown as “Not available from this source” instead of being guessed. The insight is as much about what is missing as what is present: users learn where evidence is strong, where it is thin, and what to ask next.

Benefits and intended impact

GRAVIFIRE brings investigation summaries, experimental conditions, source records and limitations into one workflow. Fire has been among spaceflight’s gravest risks, from Apollo 1 and Mir to the Artemis II smoke alarm, and no partial-gravity combustion data exists yet in PSI.

  • Researchers and engineers find relevant investigations faster, compare conditions clearly and see evidence gaps that can guide future experiments.
  • Students and educators get a story-driven way to teach scientific reasoning and why microgravity results cannot be blindly extended to other environments.
  • Earth benefits too, since NASA fire research has already improved terrestrial detection, suppression and firefighter gear.

Our intended impact is better-informed research and learning: clearer evidence, fewer unsupported extrapolations and more transparent scientific communication. GRAVIFIRE does not certify material safety or predict spacecraft fires.

Tools and development

  • Stack: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React and Tailwind CSS, hosted on Vercel.
  • Interactive 3D: React Three Fiber, Three.js, Rapier and PlayCanvas power the ISV Vesta environment in the browser.
  • Reliable by design: ranking, condition matching and EMBER’s retrieval are deterministic and cite their sources, so the same question gives the same traceable answer and nothing is invented. Vitest, Playwright and accessibility checks support quality.
  • Tooling: pnpm and Git/GitHub. The project is software-based and requires no custom hardware.
  • SI in development: OpenAI ChatGPT and Codex served as Super Intelligence (SI) development assistants for code generation and revision, research organization, ingestion and validation tooling, tests, documentation and capture automation. Their use is acknowledged in our documentation and machine-readable metadata. Original NASA measurements and source media are never represented as SI-generated.

Creativity and design considerations

GRAVIFIRE combines a scientific evidence dashboard with a narrative learning experience. Its creativity lies in making provenance, uncertainty and research limitations part of the interaction: users investigate why evidence applies, where conditions differ and what remains unanswered.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, source traceability, accessible presentation, reproducible ranking and the distinction between research relevance and safety validation. We paid particular attention to missing measurements and the limits of transferring microgravity findings to lunar or Martian conditions. These considerations shaped a platform that encourages exploration while keeping its claims bounded by the available evidence.
